By harvesting a patient’s own cells, delivering the editing machinery along with a “corrected” DNA template, and reinfusing the repaired cells, researchers can now **“infect”** humans with their own DNA to fix disease-causing mutations.\n\n---\n\n## Mechanism of Action\n\n1. **Targeted DNA Break**  \n   - A guide RNA directs Cas9 (or a Cas variant) to a specific genomic locus, where it makes a double-strand break.  \n   - Cells repair this via non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) or homology-directed repair (HDR).  \n\n2. **Homology-Directed Repair (HDR)**  \n   - When a donor DNA template with homology arms is provided, the cell’s repair machinery copies in the corrected sequence at the break site.  \n\n3. **Base & Prime Editing**  \n   - **Base editors** convert single bases (e.g. A→G or C→T) without double-strand breaks.  \n   - **Prime editors** reverse-transcribe edits from an extended guide RNA, also avoiding classic breaks.  \n\n[Learn more about HDR, base editing, and prime editing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_editing).\n\n---\n\n## Delivery Approaches\n\n| Approach     | Description                                                                                              | Examples                                                                         |\n|--------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|\n| **Ex vivo**  | Harvest patient cells (e.g. hematopoietic stem cells), edit in culture (electroporation or viral vector), then reinfuse. | CTX001/Casgevy for sickle cell & β-thalassemia                                     |\n| **In vivo**  | Direct infusion of vectors or nanoparticles carrying editors (± donor DNA) into the patient.              | EDIT-101 (retina) • NTLA-2001 (liver)                                              |\n\n---\n\n## Clinical Implementations\n\n### Ex vivo Therapy: CTX001 / Casgevy  \n- **Active Ingredient:** Exagamglogene autotemcel (CTX001; brand name **Casgevy**)  \n- **Indications:**  \n  - Sickle cell disease (SCD) with recurrent vaso-occlusive crises  \n  - Transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia  \n- **Mechanism:** CRISPR–Cas9 targets the BCL11A enhancer to reactivate fetal hemoglobin (HbF).  \n- **Approval & Rollout:**  \n  - **FDA approval:** December 8, 2023 ([press release](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-gene-therapies-treat-patients-sickle-cell-disease))  \n  - **MHRA (UK):** November 16, 2023; NHS rollout at specialist centers  \n  - **ClinicalTrials.gov:** [NCT05329649](https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT05329649)  \n\n### In vivo Therapy: EDIT-101  \n- **Indication:** Leber congenital amaurosis 10 (LCA10)  \n- **Method:** AAV-SaCas9 + guide RNA + donor template via subretinal injection  \n- **Status:** Phase 1/2 trial [NCT03872479](https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT03872479)  \n\n### In vivo Therapy: NTLA-2001  \n- **Indication:** Hereditary transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy  \n- **Method:** Lipid nanoparticles deliver Cas9 mRNA + guide RNA; gene knockout via NHEJ  \n- **Key Data:** Single dose yields > 90 % TTR knockdown for 4–6 months  \n- **Status:** Phase 1 [NCT04601051](https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT04601051) → Phase 3 MAGNITUDE trial  \n\n---\n\n## Practical Usage in Patients\n\n- **CTX001/Casgevy** is **commercially available** in the US and UK.  \n  - Administered at accredited transplant centers.  \n  - Requires myeloablative conditioning (chemotherapy) before reinfusion.  \n  - Patients typically remain hospitalized for several weeks.\n\n- **EDIT-101** and **NTLA-2001** remain **investigational**; administered in specialized trial centers.\n\n---\n\n## Cost of Therapy\n\n### United States  \n- **Casgevy list price:** \\$2.2 million USD per one-time treatment  \n- **Payment models:**  \n  - Specialty pharmacy hubs  \n  - Outcomes-based agreements  \n  - Installment plans with pay-for-performance clauses  \n\n> Source: [BioPharma Dive](https://www.biopharmadive.com/news/crispr-sickle-cell-price-millions-gene-therapy-vertex/702066/)\n\n### United Kingdom  \n- **NHS list price:** £1.65 million GBP per patient (via Innovative Medicines Fund)  \n- **Coverage:** Confidential discount agreement; up to ~ 460 eligible patients  \n- **Centres:** Seven NHS specialist centres across England  \n\n> Source: [Nature Biotechnology](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-023-02415-8)\n\n---\n\n## Future Directions\n\n1. **Improving HDR efficiency** in non-dividing cells  \n2. **Next-gen editors** with reduced off-target activity  \n3. **Non-viral delivery platforms** (LNPs, nanoparticles) to broaden tissue targeting  \n4. **Cost reduction** through manufacturing scale-up and platform optimization  \n\n---\n\n## Conclusion\n\nCRISPR-based autologous gene therapies represent a paradigm shift: patients receive their own genetically corrected cells to cure—or significantly ameliorate—their disease.  With **Casgevy** already in clinical practice at a list price near \\$2 million, and multiple in vivo therapies advancing through trials, this technology is poised to transform medicine, making “infecting” oneself with one’s own DNA not just theory, but reality.\n\n---\n\n## References\n\n1. By harvesting a patient’s own cells, delivering the editing machinery along with a “corrected” DNA template, and reinfusing the repaired cells, researchers can now **“infect”** humans with their own DNA to fix disease-causing mutations.\n\n---\n\n## Mechanism of Action\n\n1. **Targeted DNA Break**  \n   - A guide RNA directs Cas9 (or a Cas variant) to a specific genomic locus, where it makes a double-strand break.  \n   - Cells repair this via non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) or homology-directed repair (HDR).  \n\n2. **Homology-Directed Repair (HDR)**  \n   - When a donor DNA template with homology arms is provided, the cell’s repair machinery copies in the corrected sequence at the break site.  \n\n3. **Base & Prime Editing**  \n   - **Base editors** convert single bases (e.g. A→G or C→T) without double-strand breaks.  \n   - **Prime editors** reverse-transcribe edits from an extended guide RNA, also avoiding classic breaks.  \n\n[Learn more about HDR, base editing, and prime editing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_editing).\n\n---\n\n## Delivery Approaches\n\n| Approach     | Description                                                                                              | Examples                                                                         |\n|--------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|\n| **Ex vivo**  | Harvest patient cells (e.g. hematopoietic stem cells), edit in culture (electroporation or viral vector), then reinfuse. | CTX001/Casgevy for sickle cell & β-thalassemia                                     |\n| **In vivo**  | Direct infusion of vectors or nanoparticles carrying editors (± donor DNA) into the patient.              | EDIT-101 (retina) • NTLA-2001 (liver)                                              |\n\n---\n\n## Clinical Implementations\n\n### Ex vivo Therapy: CTX001 / Casgevy  \n- **Active Ingredient:** Exagamglogene autotemcel (CTX001; brand name **Casgevy**)  \n- **Indications:**  \n  - Sickle cell disease (SCD) with recurrent vaso-occlusive crises  \n  - Transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia  \n- **Mechanism:** CRISPR–Cas9 targets the BCL11A enhancer to reactivate fetal hemoglobin (HbF).  \n- **Approval & Rollout:**  \n  - **FDA approval:** December 8, 2023 ([press release](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-gene-therapies-treat-patients-sickle-cell-disease))  \n  - **MHRA (UK):** November 16, 2023; NHS rollout at specialist centers  \n  - **ClinicalTrials.gov:** [NCT05329649](https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT05329649)  \n\n### In vivo Therapy: EDIT-101  \n- **Indication:** Leber congenital amaurosis 10 (LCA10)  \n- **Method:** AAV-SaCas9 + guide RNA + donor template via subretinal injection  \n- **Status:** Phase 1/2 trial [NCT03872479](https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT03872479)  \n\n### In vivo Therapy: NTLA-2001  \n- **Indication:** Hereditary transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy  \n- **Method:** Lipid nanoparticles deliver Cas9 mRNA + guide RNA; gene knockout via NHEJ  \n- **Key Data:** Single dose yields > 90 % TTR knockdown for 4–6 months  \n- **Status:** Phase 1 [NCT04601051](https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT04601051) → Phase 3 MAGNITUDE trial  \n\n---\n\n## Practical Usage in Patients\n\n- **CTX001/Casgevy** is **commercially available** in the US and UK.  \n  - Administered at accredited transplant centers.  \n  - Requires myeloablative conditioning (chemotherapy) before reinfusion.  \n  - Patients typically remain hospitalized for several weeks.\n\n- **EDIT-101** and **NTLA-2001** remain **investigational**; administered in specialized trial centers.\n\n---\n\n## Cost of Therapy\n\n### United States  \n- **Casgevy list price:** \\$2.2 million USD per one-time treatment  \n- **Payment models:**  \n  - Specialty pharmacy hubs  \n  - Outcomes-based agreements  \n  - Installment plans with pay-for-performance clauses  \n\n> Source: [BioPharma Dive](https://www.biopharmadive.com/news/crispr-sickle-cell-price-millions-gene-therapy-vertex/702066/)\n\n### United Kingdom  \n- **NHS list price:** £1.65 million GBP per patient (via Innovative Medicines Fund)  \n- **Coverage:** Confidential discount agreement; up to ~ 460 eligible patients  \n- **Centres:** Seven NHS specialist centres across England  \n\n> Source: [Nature Biotechnology](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-023-02415-8)\n\n---\n\n## Future Directions\n\n1. **Improving HDR efficiency** in non-dividing cells  \n2. **Next-gen editors** with reduced off-target activity  \n3. **Non-viral delivery platforms** (LNPs, nanoparticles) to broaden tissue targeting  \n4. **Cost reduction** through manufacturing scale-up and platform optimization  \n\n---\n\n## Conclusion\n\nCRISPR-based autologous gene therapies represent a paradigm shift: patients receive their own genetically corrected cells to cure—or significantly ameliorate—their disease.  With **Casgevy** already in clinical practice at a list price near \\$2 million, and multiple in vivo therapies advancing through trials, this technology is poised to transform medicine, making “infecting” oneself with one’s own DNA not just theory, but reality.\n\n---\n\n## References\n\n1. Robust to single-year shocks (wars, pandemics) that make\n * raw year-over-year differences noisy. Points whose trailing window holds\n * fewer than 3 samples are skipped, which naturally drops the sparse\n * pre-1950 part of the historical record.\n */\nexport function rollingSlope(points: Point[], windowYears: number): Point[] {\n  const result: Point[] = [];\n  for (let i = 0; i < points.length; i++) {\n    const windowStart = points[i].year - windowYears;\n    const window = points.filter((p) => p.year > windowStart && p.year <= points[i].year);\n    if (window.length < 3) continue;\n    result.push({ year: points[i].year, value: olsSlope(window) });\n  }\n  return result;\n}\n\n/** Velocity of life expectancy growth, smoothed over a trailing window. */\nexport function velocity(series: Point[], windowYears = 10): Point[] {\n  return rollingSlope(series, windowYears);\n}\n\n/** Acceleration: derivative of the smoothed velocity, smoothed the same way. */\nexport function acceleration(series: Point[], windowYears = 10): Point[] {\n  return rollingSlope(velocity(series, windowYears), windowYears);\n}\n\nexport interface LevAssessment {\n  /** Latest smoothed velocity, in years of life expectancy per calendar year. */\n  currentVelocity: number;\n  /** Year of the latest observation the assessment is based on. */\n  asOfYear: number;\n  /** Fraction of the LEV threshold currently reached (0..1+). */\n  progress: number;\n  /** Trend of the velocity itself over the fit window (per year). */\n  velocityTrend: number;\n  /** True when the latest velocity already meets the threshold. */\n  reached: boolean;\n  /**\n   * Extrapolated calendar year when velocity reaches the threshold, following\n   * the current trend. Null when the trend is flat or negative — on the\n   * current trajectory the threshold is never reached.\n   */\n  etaYear: number | null;\n}\n\n/**\n * Assess progress toward longevity escape velocity from a smoothed velocity\n * series: how fast are we, is the velocity itself rising, and if the recent\n * trend holds, when does v(t) cross the threshold?\n */\nexport function assessLev(\n  velocityPoints: Point[],\n  fitWindowYears = 30,\n  threshold = LEV_THRESHOLD\n): LevAssessment | null {\n  if (velocityPoints.length === 0) return null;\n  const latest = velocityPoints[velocityPoints.length - 1];\n  const fitWindow = velocityPoints.filter((p) => p.year > latest.year - fitWindowYears);\n  if (fitWindow.length < 3) return null;\n\n  const trend = olsSlope(fitWindow);\n  const reached = latest.value >= threshold;\n  let etaYear: number | null = null;\n  if (reached) {\n    etaYear = latest.year;\n  } else if (trend > 1e-6) {\n    etaYear = Math.round(latest.year + (threshold - latest.value) / trend);\n  }\n\n  return {\n    currentVelocity: latest.value,\n    asOfYear: latest.year,\n    progress: Math.max(0, latest.value / threshold),\n    velocityTrend: trend,\n    reached,\n    etaYear,\n  };\n}\nexport interface Snapshot {\n  source: string;\n  sourceUrl: string;\n  fetchedAt: string;\n  entities: string[];\n  series: By harvesting a patient’s own cells, delivering the editing machinery along with a “corrected” DNA template, and reinfusing the repaired cells, researchers can now **“infect”** humans with their own DNA to fix disease-causing mutations.\n\n---\n\n## Mechanism of Action\n\n1. **Targeted DNA Break**  \n   - **Prime editors** reverse-transcribe edits from an extended guide RNA, also avoiding classic breaks.  \n\n[Learn more about HDR, base editing, and prime editing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_editing).\n\n---\n\n## Delivery Approaches\n\n| Approach     | Description                                                                                              | Examples                                                                         |\n|--------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|\n| **Ex vivo**  | Harvest patient cells (e.g. hematopoietic stem cells), edit in culture (electroporation or viral vector), then reinfuse. | CTX001/Casgevy for sickle cell & β-thalassemia                                     |\n| **In vivo**  | Direct infusion of vectors or nanoparticles carrying editors (± donor DNA) into the patient.              | EDIT-101 (retina) • NTLA-2001 (liver)                                              |\n\n---\n\n## Clinical Implementations\n\n### Ex vivo Therapy: CTX001 / Casgevy  \n- **Active Ingredient:** Exagamglogene autotemcel (CTX001; brand name **Casgevy**)  \n- **Indications:**  \n  - [2026-10-22T17:53:17.615Z] [INFO]         "content": "CRISPR-Autologous-Gene-Therapy.md\nLICENSE\nREADME.md\napp\ndocs\nexperiments\ndocs/case-studies:\nissue-7\n\ndocs/case-studies/issue-7:\nissue-comments.json\nissue.json\npr-8.json\n     1\t# CRISPR-Based Autologous Gene Therapy: Using Your Own DNA to Repair Damaged Cells\n     2\t\n     3\t**Published:** May 1, 2025  \n     4\t**Format:** Markdown (for GitHub)\n     5\t\n     6\t---\n     7\t\n     8\t## Introduction\n     9\t\n    10\tCRISPR–Cas9 and its derivative technologies (base editors, prime editors) have ushered in a new era of precision gene therapy.  By harvesting a patient’s own cells, delivering the editing machinery along with a “corrected” DNA template, and reinfusing the repaired cells, researchers can now **“infect”** humans with their own DNA to fix disease-causing mutations.\n    11\t\n    12\t---\n    13\t\n    14\t## Mechanism of Action\n    15\t\n    16\t1. **Targeted DNA Break**  \n    17\t   - A guide RNA directs Cas9 (or a Cas variant) to a specific genomic locus, where it makes a double-strand break.  \n    18\t   - Cells repair this via non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) or homology-directed repair (HDR).  \n    19\t\n    20\t2. **Homology-Directed Repair (HDR)**  \n    21\t   - When a donor DNA template with homology arms is provided, the cell’s repair machinery copies in the corrected sequence at the break site.  \n    22\t\n    23\t3. **Base & Prime Editing**  \n    24\t   - **Base editors** convert single bases (e.g. A→G or C→T) without double-strand breaks.  \n    25\t   - **Prime editors** reverse-transcribe edits from an extended guide RNA, also avoiding classic breaks.  \n    26\t\n    27\t[Learn more about HDR, base editing, and prime editing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_editing).\n    28\t\n    29\t---\n    30\t\n    31\t## Delivery Approaches\n    32\t\n    33\t| Approach     | Description                                                                                              | Examples                                                                         |\n    34\t|--------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|\n    35\t| **Ex vivo**  | Harvest patient cells (e.g. hematopoietic stem cells), edit in culture (electroporation or viral vector), then reinfuse. | CTX001/Casgevy for sickle cell & β-thalassemia                                     |\n    36\t| **In vivo**  | Direct infusion of vectors or nanoparticles carrying editors (± donor DNA) into the patient.              | EDIT-101 (retina) • NTLA-2001 (liver)                                              |\n    37\t\n    38\t---\n    39\t\n    40\t## Clinical Implementations\n    41\t\n    42\t### Ex vivo Therapy: CTX001 / Casgevy  \n    43\t- **Active Ingredient:** Exagamglogene autotemcel (CTX001; brand name **Casgevy**)  \n    44\t- **Indications:**  \n    45\t  - Sickle cell disease (SCD) with recurrent vaso-occlusive crises  \n    46\t  - Transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia  \n    47\t- **Mechanism:** CRISPR–Cas9 targets the BCL11A enhancer to reactivate fetal hemoglobin (HbF).  \n    48\t- **Approval & Rollout:**  \n    49\t  - **FDA approval:** December 8, 2023 ([press release](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-gene-therapies-treat-patients-sickle-cell-disease))  \n    50\t  - **MHRA (UK):** November 16, 2023; NHS rollout at specialist centers  \n    51\t  - **ClinicalTrials.gov:** [NCT05329649](https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT05329649)  \n    52\t\n    53\t### In vivo Therapy: EDIT-101  \n    54\t- **Indication:** Leber congenital amaurosis 10 (LCA10)  \n    55\t- **Method:** AAV-SaCas9 + guide RNA + donor template via subretinal injection  \n    56\t- **Status:** Phase 1/2 trial [NCT03872479](https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT03872479)  \n    57\t\n    58\t### In vivo Therapy: NTLA-2001  \n    59\t- **Indication:** Hereditary transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy  \n    60\t- **Method:** Lipid nanoparticles deliver Cas9 mRNA + guide RNA; gene knockout via NHEJ  \n    61\t- **Key Data:** Single dose yields > 90 % TTR knockdown for 4–6 months  \n    62\t- **Status:** Phase 1 [NCT04601051](https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT04601051) → Phase 3 MAGNITUDE trial  \n    63\t\n    64\t---\n    65\t\n    66\t## Practical Usage in Patients\n    67\t\n    68\t- **CTX001/Casgevy** is **commercially available** in the US and UK.  \n    69\t  - Administered at accredited transplant centers.  \n    70\t  - Requires myeloablative conditioning (chemotherapy) before reinfusion.  \n    71\t  - Patients typically remain hospitalized for several weeks.\n    72\t\n    73\t- **EDIT-101** and **NTLA-2001** remain **investigational**; administered in specialized trial centers.\n    74\t\n    75\t---\n    76\t\n    77\t## Cost of Therapy\n    78\t\n    79\t### United States  \n    80\t- **Casgevy list price:** \\$2.2 million USD per one-time treatment  \n    81\t- **Payment models:**  \n    82\t  - Specialty pharmacy hubs  \n    83\t  - Outcomes-based agreements  \n    84\t  - Installment plans with pay-for-performance clauses  \n    85\t\n    86\t> Source: [BioPharma Dive](https://www.biopharmadive.com/news/crispr-sickle-cell-price-millions-gene-therapy-vertex/702066/)\n    87\t\n    88\t### United Kingdom  \n    89\t- **NHS list price:** £1.65 million GBP per patient (via Innovative Medicines Fund)  \n    90\t- **Coverage:** Confidential discount agreement; up to ~ 460 eligible patients  \n    91\t- **Centres:** Seven NHS specialist centres across England  \n    92\t\n    93\t> Source: [Nature Biotechnology](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-023-02415-8)\n    94\t\n    95\t---\n    96\t\n    97\t## Future Directions\n    98\t\n    99\t1. **Improving HDR efficiency** in non-dividing cells  \n   100\t2. **Next-gen editors** with reduced off-target activity  \n   101\t3. **Non-viral delivery platforms** (LNPs, nanoparticles) to broaden tissue targeting  \n   102\t4. **Cost reduction** through manufacturing scale-up and platform optimization  \n   103\t\n   104\t---\n   105\t\n   106\t## Conclusion\n   107\t\n   108\tCRISPR-based autologous gene therapies represent a paradigm shift: patients receive their own genetically corrected cells to cure—or significantly ameliorate—their disease.  With **Casgevy** already in clinical practice at a list price near \\$2 million, and multiple in vivo therapies advancing through trials, this technology is poised to transform medicine, making “infecting” oneself with one’s own DNA not just theory, but reality.\n   109\t\n   110\t---\n   111\t\n   112\t## References\n   113\t\n   114\t1. Caldwell's review of the paper reports that factors exogenous to a country's current level of income probably account for 75–90 per cent of the growth in life expectancy for the world as a whole between the 1930s and the 1960s. That leaves income accounting for roughly the 10–25 percent you mentioned. Preston's counterfactual was that income alone would have produced a much smaller gain, about 2.5 years over the three decades instead of the observed 12.2 years (index 2-5). Caldwell adds that this pattern held for both industrialized and developing countries (index 2-7).\n\nThe paper's core evidence is a scatter diagram of life expectancy against national income per head for the 1900s, 1930s, and 1960s (index 5-4). Preston read the upward shift of that curve over time as the effect of medical progress and health care beyond income (index 1-2). Later work has disputed this. Economists such as Pritchett and Summers argued that income growth eventually feeds into education and health services, so its importance is understated when time is not modeled properly (index 2-11). Verbatim definition: \"mortality rates fall so fast that people's remaining (not merely total) life expectancy increases with time … it is simply the ratio of the mortality rates at consecutive ages (in the same year) in the age range where most people die, which is only about 10% per year. I term this rate of reduction of age-specific mortality risk 'actuarial escape velocity' (AEV)\". He explicitly notes period LE is \"a purely artificial construction\".\n- de Grey et al. 2002, Ann NY Acad Sci, \"Time to Talk SENS\", 10.1111/j.1749-6632.2002.tb02115.x.\n- Warner et al. 2005, EMBO Rep, \"Science fact and the SENS agenda\", 10.1038/sj.embor.7400555 (critique by 28 gerontologists).\n- Kurzweil predicts LEV around 2029 (\"between 2029 and 2035\"; \"getting back about four months a year\") in The Singularity Is Nearer (2024).\n- Conclusion: LEV is a speculative hypothesis, not a consensus. Period e0 +1 yr/yr is neither necessary nor sufficient for AEV: e0 is dominated by young-age mortality, and remaining LE at age x declines by less than 1 per year of age. A better formalization is the annual % decline in age-specific mortality at ages 60–90 compared with the Gompertz slope (~8–10%/yr), or the change in e_x(t) for a fixed birth cohort. Historical old-age mortality declines are about 1–2%/yr (Kannisto 1994; Vaupel 2010).\n\nAging interventions:\n- Senolytics:\n  - UBX0101 Phase 2 knee OA failed, Aug 2020 (Osteoarthritis Cartilage 2021 abstract, 10.1016/j.joca.2021.02.077).\n  - Unity UBX1325 ASPIRE missed its primary non-inferiority endpoint. [2026-10-22T18:17:19.631Z] [INFO]           "content": "# Issue #7: verifying the science behind the immortality claims\n\nChecked on 2026-10-22, for [konard/immortality issue #7](https://github.com/konard/immortality/issues/7) (\"Double check correctness of all conclusions about immortality\").\n\n## Method and rules used\n\n- **Evidence ranking.** Primary sources come first:\n  - peer-reviewed papers with DOIs (checked against Crossref or Europe PMC wherever possible)\n  - regulator notices (FDA, EMA, MHRA, NICE / NHS England)\n  - ClinicalTrials.gov records, read through the v2 API (`https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/{NCT}`)\n  - company filings with the US SEC (8-K exhibits)\n\n  Trade press is used only when no primary source was reachable. In that case the source is labelled as secondary.\n- **Consensus rule (from the issue).** A conclusion is called *likely* only when several independent groups, ideally in different countries, agree. A single paper with no independent replication is labelled **Unconfirmed-single-study**, however prestigious its venue.\n- **Verdicts.**\n  - **Confirmed:** correct as written.\n  - **Corrected:** factually wrong, with a fix proposed.\n  - **Outdated:** correct when written, but superseded by later events.\n  - **Unconfirmed-single-study:** rests on one study or one group.\n  - **Speculative:** a hypothesis with no empirical consensus.\n- **What could not be verified is said explicitly.** It is also listed in the section \"Items that could not be verified\" at the end. No citation, DOI or date below was invented. Where a DOI was not confirmed through Crossref or Europe PMC, the reference says so.\n- **Dashboard numbers.** These were recomputed with a script that reimplements `rollingSlope` (10-year trailing OLS, `SMOOTH_WINDOW = 10`, `app/src/App.tsx:41`) and `assessLev` (30-year trend fit, `app/src/analytics.ts:102-129`). The script ran on the repository snapshot `app/public/data/life-expectancy.json`: OWID \"Life expectancy at birth (period)\", fetched 2026-08-10. The latest data year in that snapshot is **2023**.\n\n---\n\n## Claim 1: `CRISPR-Autologous-Gene-Therapy.md` (dated May 1, 2025)\n\n### 1.1 Introduction: \"corrected DNA template\" and \"infect\"\n\n> \"By harvesting a patient’s own cells, delivering the editing machinery along with a “corrected” DNA template, and reinfusing the repaired cells, researchers can now **“infect”** humans with their own DNA to fix disease-causing mutations.\" (`CRISPR-Autologous-Gene-Therapy.md:10`)\n\n**Verdict: Corrected.**\n\n**Evidence**\n\n- **Casgevy (exa-cel) uses no donor template.**\n  - Patient CD34+ cells are electroporated with a Cas9–sgRNA ribonucleoprotein.\n  - The Cas9 cut, repaired by error-prone NHEJ, disrupts a GATA1 binding site in the erythroid-specific enhancer of *BCL11A*.\n  - Fetal haemoglobin (HbF) then rises. The disease-causing *HBB* mutation is not corrected [6, 7, 8].\n- **EDIT-101 also uses no donor template.** Its two guides delete the intronic *CEP290* IVS26 variant [18].\n- **NTLA-2001 / nex-z also uses no donor template.** It is an NHEJ knockout of *TTR* [20, 21].\n- **None of the three marketed or late-stage examples in the document uses HDR with a donor template.**\n- **\"Infect\" is a misnomer.**\n  - Casgevy involves no virus at all.\n  - The cells are the patient's own (autologous), edited outside the body, and returned after myeloablative busulfan conditioning.\n- **Consensus.** The mechanism is described the same way by:\n  - the pivotal trial reports (multinational: US, Canada, Europe, Middle East) [7, 8]\n  - FDA [1], EMA [3] and MHRA [2]\n\n  This is uncontested.\n\n**Proposed wording**\n\n> CRISPR–Cas9 and its derivative technologies (base editors, prime editors) have ushered in a new era of precision gene therapy. In the *ex vivo* approach, a patient’s own blood stem cells are collected, edited outside the body, and reinfused after chemotherapy conditioning. The first approved CRISPR medicine, Casgevy, does not insert a corrected gene. It uses a single Cas9 cut to switch off the *BCL11A* erythroid enhancer, so red cells make fetal haemoglobin again. *In vivo* approaches instead deliver the editor directly into the body (e.g. by lipid nanoparticles to the liver).\n\nIn the conclusion (line 108), replace \"making “infecting” oneself …\" with \"making treatment with one’s own edited cells …\".\n\n### 1.2 Mechanism section (HDR, base and prime editing)\n\n> \"Cells repair this via non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) or homology-directed repair (HDR)\" / \"Base editors convert single bases (e.g. A→G or C→T) without double-strand breaks\" / \"Prime editors reverse-transcribe edits from an extended guide RNA, also avoiding classic breaks.\" (`CRISPR-Autologous-Gene-Therapy.md:16-25`)\n\n**Verdict: Confirmed**, with one clarification.\n\n**Evidence**\n\n- The general mechanism text is textbook-correct.\n- Prime editors nick one DNA strand rather than leaving the DNA uncut.\n- In vivo base editing has now been used clinically:\n  - the \"baby KJ\" CPS1-deficiency case: LNP-delivered adenine base editor, NEJM 2025, one patient [27, 28]\n  - the first prime-editing human data: Prime Medicine PM359, ex vivo, p47phox chronic granulomatous disease, two patients, NEJM, December 2025 [29]\n\n  Both are **Unconfirmed-single-study**: one or two patients each, no replication yet.\n\n**Proposed wording (add after line 25)**\n\n> Clinically, most approved or late-stage CRISPR therapies use NHEJ gene disruption rather than HDR correction. The first in-vivo base-editing treatment, a personalised editor for one infant with CPS1 deficiency, was reported in 2025 (Musunuru et al., NEJM). The first prime-editing patient data (two patients with p47phox chronic granulomatous disease) were also reported in 2025. Both are single-patient or two-patient reports, not yet replicated.\n\n### 1.3 Delivery table\n\n> \"edit in culture (electroporation or viral vector)\" (`:35`); \"Direct infusion of vectors or nanoparticles carrying editors (± donor DNA)\" (`:36`)\n\n**Verdict: Confirmed** in general. For Casgevy specifically it should say *electroporation*: there is no viral vector [6].\n\nThe in-vivo row lists EDIT-101 under \"infusion\". EDIT-101 is actually a **subretinal injection** of AAV5 [18].\n\n**Proposed wording**\n\n- Ex vivo row: \"edit in culture (for Casgevy: electroporation of Cas9–guide RNA complexes; some other products use viral vectors)\".\n- In vivo row: \"Direct delivery of editors into the body, e.g. intravenous lipid nanoparticles (NTLA-2001) or subretinal AAV injection (EDIT-101)\".\n\n### 1.4 Casgevy mechanism and indications\n\n> \"CRISPR–Cas9 targets the BCL11A enhancer to reactivate fetal hemoglobin (HbF).\" (`:47`); indications SCD with recurrent VOCs and transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia (`:44-46`)\n\n**Verdict: Confirmed** [1, 3, 7, 8].\n\nThe age limits have changed (see 1.5).\n\n### 1.5 Casgevy approvals and dates\n\n> \"**FDA approval:** December 8, 2023\" (`:49`); \"**MHRA (UK):** November 16, 2023; NHS rollout at specialist centers\" (`:50`)\n\n**Verdict: Confirmed (dates) / Outdated (scope).**\n\n**Evidence**\n\n| Event | Date | Source |\n|---|---|---|\n| MHRA conditional marketing authorisation, SCD and TDT, ages 12+ (world first) | 16 Nov 2023 | gov.uk [2] |\n| FDA approval, SCD, ages 12+ (same day as bluebird's Lyfgenia, lovo-cel) | 8 Dec 2023 | FDA [1] |\n| FDA approval, TDT, ages 12+ (ahead of the 30 Mar 2024 PDUFA date) | 16 Jan 2024 | [5] (secondary; the FDA notice was not separately retrieved) |\n| EMA CHMP positive opinion | Dec 2023 | PEI [4] |\n| EU conditional marketing authorisation | 9 Feb 2024 | EMA EPAR [3] |\n| FDA label expanded to ages 2+ (SCD and TDT), based on CLIMB-151 / CLIMB-141; approved 53 days after filing, under a Commissioner's National Priority Voucher | announced 1 Jul 2026 | Vertex 8-K [11]; Healio [12] |\n| Approved in 39 countries (North America, Europe, Middle East) | as of Q2 2026 | Vertex 8-K [11] |\n\n**Consensus.** Regulatory facts are primary-source facts; no replication is needed.\n\n**Proposed wording (replace lines 49-50)**\n\n> - **MHRA (UK):** conditional authorisation 16 November 2023 (world first; ages 12+)\n> - **FDA (US):** SCD approved 8 December 2023 (same day as bluebird bio’s lentiviral Lyfgenia); TDT approved 16 January 2024; label expanded to patients aged 2 years and older in July 2026\n> - **EU:** conditional marketing authorisation 9 February 2024\n> - By mid-2026 Casgevy was approved in 39 countries (Vertex, Q2 2026 results).\n\n### 1.6 ClinicalTrials.gov number\n\n> \"**ClinicalTrials.gov:** [NCT05329649]\" (`:51`); reference 4 \"ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05329649 (CTX001)\" (`:120`)\n\n**Verdict: Corrected (mislabelled).**\n\n**Evidence (ClinicalTrials.gov API records)**\n\n| NCT | Study | Phase | Enrollment | Status |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| NCT05329649 [13a] | CLIMB-151: \"Evaluation of Safety and Efficacy of CTX001 in Pediatric Participants With Severe Sickle Cell Disease\" | 3 | 13 | Active, not recruiting (last update 2026-07-01) |\n| NCT03655678 [13b] | CLIMB-111 (TDT), pivotal trial behind the approvals | 2/3 | 59 | Completed |\n| NCT03745287 [13c] | CLIMB-121 (SCD), pivotal trial behind the approvals | 2/3 | 63 | Completed |\n| NCT05356195 [13d] | CLIMB-141, paediatric TDT | 3 | 16 | Active, not recruiting |\n\nSo NCT05329649 is a real CTX001 trial, but it is the paediatric SCD study, not the trial behind the 2023 approvals.\n\n**Proposed wording**\n\n> **Pivotal trials:** CLIMB-121 (SCD, [NCT03745287](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03745287)) and CLIMB-111 (TDT, [NCT03655678](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03655678)). Paediatric studies CLIMB-151 ([NCT05329649](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05329649)) and CLIMB-141 ([NCT05356195](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05356195)) supported the 2026 label expansion to ages 2+.\n\nAlso update reference 4. The `ct2/show` URLs still redirect, but the current form is `clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT…`.\n\n### 1.7 EDIT-101\n\n> \"**Method:** AAV-SaCas9 + guide RNA + donor template via subretinal injection\" (`:55`); \"**Status:** Phase 1/2 trial NCT03872479\" (`:56`); \"EDIT-101 and NTLA-2001 remain investigational\" (`:73`)\n\n**Verdict: Corrected (method) and Outdated (status).**\n\n**Evidence**\n\n- **Method.**\n  - EDIT-101 is an AAV5 vector encoding *S. aureus* Cas9 and **two** guide RNAs.\n  - The guides excise or invert the intronic IVS26 (c.2991+1655A>G) variant that creates a cryptic splice site.\n  - **There is no donor template** [18].\n- **BRILLIANCE results.** Pierce et al., NEJM 2024 [18]:\n  - 14 participants (12 adults, 2 children).\n  - No serious adverse events related to treatment or procedure.\n  - Some participants improved on at least one measure, but only a minority met the pre-set responder threshold.\n- **Status.**\n  - In November 2022 Editas paused enrollment and said it would seek a partner. It cited 3 of 14 patients meeting the responder threshold and a small addressable population, about 300 US IVS26 homozygotes [19].\n  - Editas then stopped internal investment in the programme (secondary source [19]).\n  - ClinicalTrials.gov still shows NCT03872479 with status \"UNKNOWN\" (last update 2022-12-05) [13e].\n  - No restart was found as of October 2026.\n- **Consensus.** This is a single trial from one sponsor (US sites). Its efficacy conclusions are **Unconfirmed-single-study**.\n\n**Proposed wording**\n\n> - **Method:** AAV5 vector carrying SaCas9 and two guide RNAs that cut out the IVS26 splice mutation (no donor template), given by subretinal injection\n> - **Status:** Phase 1/2 BRILLIANCE trial ([NCT03872479](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03872479)); results in 14 participants published in NEJM 2024 (Pierce et al.): acceptable safety, improvement in a minority. Editas paused the programme in November 2022 to seek a partner; no further development has been announced.\n\n### 1.8 NTLA-2001 / nexiguran ziclumeran (nex-z)\n\n> \"**Indication:** Hereditary transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy\" (`:59`); \"**Key Data:** Single dose yields > 90 % TTR knockdown for 4–6 months\" (`:61`); \"**Status:** Phase 1 NCT04601051 → Phase 3 MAGNITUDE trial\" (`:62`)\n\n**Verdict: Outdated / incomplete.**\n\n**Evidence**\n\n- **Indication.**\n  - The Phase 1 trial NCT04601051 enrolled both hereditary ATTR with polyneuropathy (ATTRv-PN) and ATTR cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM): 72 participants, completed, last update 2026-01-30 [13f].\n  - The ATTR-CM cohort includes **wild-type** (non-hereditary) disease, not only hereditary disease [21].\n- **Data.**\n  - The first report showed a mean 87% serum TTR reduction at day 28 with 0.3 mg/kg [20].\n  - The ATTR-CM cohort (n=36) showed about 90% mean reduction sustained through 12 months [21].\n  - Two-year PN data from Intellia show durable reductions (company data [22a], not separately peer-reviewed at 2 years).\n  - So \"4–6 months\" understates the durability observed.\n- **Phase 3 programme.**\n  - MAGNITUDE, ATTR-CM: NCT06128629, about 1,200 planned, recruiting [13g].\n  - MAGNITUDE-2, ATTRv-PN: NCT06672237, about 60 planned, recruiting [13h].\n- **Safety event and clinical holds.**\n  - 27 Oct 2025: Intellia disclosed a Grade 4 transaminase and bilirubin elevation in a MAGNITUDE participant dosed 30 Sep 2025.\n  - 29 Oct 2025: FDA placed both Phase 3 trials on clinical hold.\n  - 5 Nov 2025: the participant died. Intellia later attributed the death to sepsis after a gastrointestinal complication, which is the company's account [22].\n  - 27 Jan 2026: the MAGNITUDE-2 hold was lifted [23].\n  - 2 Mar 2026: the MAGNITUDE hold was lifted. Conditions included enhanced liver monitoring, steroid-management guidance and exclusion of patients with liver abnormalities [24, 25].\n  - Intellia's 6 Aug 2026 Q2 report states \"Enrollment successfully reinitiated in nex-z Phase 3 clinical trials\". MAGNITUDE-2 enrollment is expected to complete in H2 2026 [26].\n  - Nex-z is co-developed with Regeneron.\n- **Related development.** Intellia's second in-vivo CRISPR product, lonvo-z (NTLA-2002, hereditary angioedema), reported positive Phase 3 HAELO data in NEJM. Intellia expects FDA to accept its BLA in H2 2026 and a US launch in H1 2027 [26]. If approved, it would be the first approved **in vivo** CRISPR therapy. As of 2026-10-22 it is **not approved**.\n- **Consensus.** The TTR knockdown data come from one sponsor's trial run at sites in several countries (UK, New Zealand, Sweden, US and others) [20, 21]. Clinical-outcome efficacy (deaths and cardiovascular events) is **not yet shown**: that is MAGNITUDE's purpose.\n\n**Proposed wording**\n\n> ### In vivo Therapy: NTLA-2001 (nexiguran ziclumeran, “nex-z”; Intellia/Regeneron)\n> - **Indication:** Transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis — both hereditary polyneuropathy (ATTRv-PN) and cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM, hereditary or wild-type)\n> - **Method:** Lipid nanoparticles deliver Cas9 mRNA + guide RNA to the liver; *TTR* knockout via NHEJ (no donor template)\n> - **Key Data:** In the Phase 1 trial (NCT04601051, 72 participants) a single infusion lowered serum TTR by about 90% on average, sustained for at least 1–2 years. Clinical-outcome benefit is not yet proven.\n> - **Status:** Phase 3 MAGNITUDE (ATTR-CM, NCT06128629) and MAGNITUDE-2 (ATTRv-PN, NCT06672237). Both were placed on FDA clinical hold in October 2025 after a Grade 4 liver-injury event; the patient later died. The holds were lifted in January (MAGNITUDE-2) and March 2026 (MAGNITUDE), with added liver monitoring, and enrollment has resumed.\n\n### 1.9 \"Commercially available in the US and UK\"\n\n> \"**CTX001/Casgevy** is **commercially available** in the US and UK.\" (`:68`); \"Patients typically remain hospitalized for several weeks.\" (`:71`)\n\n**Verdict: Outdated.**\n\n**Evidence**\n\n- **Availability.** Casgevy was approved in 39 countries by Q2 2026 [11].\n- **Uptake was slow at first, then accelerated** (all from Vertex SEC filings):\n  - 2024: revenue $10.0 M [10].\n  - Through 30 Jun 2025: about 115 patients had a first cell collection, 29 were infused, and more than 75 authorised treatment centres were active [9].\n  - Full-year 2025: revenue $115.8 M; 64 patients infused; 147 first cell collections [10].\n  - Q2 2026: revenue $76 M, up 151% year on year [11]. On the Q2 2026 call management said H1 2026 infusions exceeded those for all of 2025. That figure is from the call, not the 8-K text, and the exact number was not verified.\n  - Vertex estimates more than 60,000 eligible patients in approved countries [10].\n- **Hospital stay.** \"Several weeks\" is consistent with the pivotal trials, where neutrophil engraftment took a median of about 4 weeks after infusion [7, 8].\n- **Conditioning toxicity.** Myeloablative busulfan conditioning is the main toxicity and a key barrier to uptake [7, 8].\n\n**Proposed wording**\n\n> - **CTX001/Casgevy** is commercially available — approved in 39 countries by mid-2026 (US, UK, EU, Canada, Switzerland, Gulf states and others). Uptake is still small relative to need: 64 patients were infused worldwide in 2025, against an estimated >60,000 eligible patients, although infusions accelerated in 2026.\n\n### 1.10 US price and payment\n\n> \"**Casgevy list price:** \\$2.2 million USD per one-time treatment\" (`:80`)\n\n**Verdict: Confirmed** [17, 16].\n\nFor context:\n\n- Lyfgenia's US list price is $3.1 M, and it carries a boxed warning for haematologic malignancy [16].\n- ICER judged Casgevy cost-effective at prices up to about $2.05 M [16] (secondary source for the ICER figure).\n- About 90% of US patients have reimbursed access, according to Vertex [10].\n- The payment-model bullets (`:81-84`) were not individually verified. He attributes this to factors exogenous to a country's own income, such as imported public-health technology.\n  - **Cutler, Deaton & Lleras-Muney (2006, US/UK)** [45]:\n    - Before 1900, nutrition and public works (clean water, sanitation) mattered most.\n    - In the early 20th century, public health, vaccination and later antibiotics drove gains.\n    - After about 1970, gains in rich countries came mainly from falling cardiovascular mortality at older ages.\n  - **Cutler & Miller (2005, US)** [46]: clean water alone accounted for about half of the urban mortality decline in early-20th-century US cities.\n  - **Omran's epidemiologic transition (Egypt/US)** [47] and **Riley (2001, US)** [52] describe the shift from infectious to chronic disease mortality, starting with infants and children.\n  - **Acemoglu & Johnson (2007, US)** [48] use the post-1940 \"international epidemiological transition\" (antibiotics, DDT, WHO campaigns) as a natural experiment.\n  - **China's 1950–80 decline** is attributed mainly to public health and education campaigns, not income (Babiarz et al. 2015, US/China team) [49].\n  - **Szreter (1988, UK)** [50] argues against attributing 19th-century British gains mostly to nutrition. He emphasises public-health intervention.\n- **Consensus.** Teams in the US, UK, Europe and China agree that the fastest secular gains came from falling infectious and child mortality in the late 19th to mid-20th centuries. Sanitation and public health are the main levers, with vaccines and antibiotics important after about 1940. They also agree that the decline in childhood mortality, not aging biology, produced those gains.\n\n**Proposed wording (TSX)**\n\n> Velocity peaked at **{peak.value} yr / yr around {peak.year}**. In single-country series such peaks are often rebounds after wars, famines or pandemics. Globally, the fastest sustained gains came in the mid-20th century, as sanitation, public health, vaccines, antibiotics and malaria control cut infant and child deaths. The 30-year trend is currently …\n\n### 2b. Longevity escape velocity: consensus or hypothesis?\n\n> \"(the point where each calendar year lived adds a full year of life expectancy, so remaining life expectancy stops shrinking)\" (`app/src/App.tsx:365-366`); \"Longevity escape velocity (LEV) is the point where v(t) >= 1: every calendar year lived adds at least one more year of remaining life expectancy.\" (`app/src/analytics.ts:8-9`)\n\n**Verdict: Speculative** (the concept), and **Corrected** (the definition used).\n\n**Evidence**\n\n- **Origin.**\n  - The concept comes from Aubrey de Grey (UK/US; de Grey 2004, PLoS Biology) [31], building on the SENS programme [32].\n  - Ray Kurzweil popularised it and predicts LEV around 2029–2035 [80].\n  - Neither is a demographic forecast based on mortality data.\n- **No peer-reviewed demographic forecast predicts LEV this century.**\n  - Major forecasting groups project world gains of about 0.14–0.16 yr/yr to 2050:\n    - UN Population Division [42]\n    - IHME / GBD, US with global collaborators [40]\n  - High-longevity forecasts reach about 0.25 yr/yr. Examples are Oeppen & Vaupel's record-LE trend (UK/Germany/Denmark) [33] and Vaupel et al. 2021 [34].\n  - Olshansky et al. 2024 (US) [35] argue gains are decelerating and that radical life extension is \"implausible\" this century unless aging itself is slowed. That is a scenario no one can yet forecast.\n- **Critique by gerontologists.** In 2005, 28 senior biogerontologists from several countries published a detailed rebuttal of the SENS agenda [37]. They did not rule out future progress, but rejected claims of imminent indefinite life extension.\n- **What de Grey actually defined.** He defined the threshold in terms of **age-specific mortality**, not period life expectancy at birth [31]. His words:\n\n  > \"mortality rates fall so fast that people's remaining (not merely total) life expectancy increases with time … the ratio of the mortality rates at consecutive ages (in the same year) in the age range where most people die, which is only about 10% per year. I term this rate of reduction of age-specific mortality risk 'actuarial escape velocity' (AEV).\"\n\n  He also calls period life expectancy \"a purely artificial construction\".\n- **Why \"remaining life expectancy stops shrinking\" does not follow from period e0 rising 1 yr/yr.**\n  - Period e0 is dominated by deaths at young ages.\n  - An individual's remaining life expectancy is e at their *current* age x, evaluated over their own future.\n  - One year later, the relevant quantity is e at age x+1 in year t+1. It can keep falling even while e0 rises fast, as happened in the mid-20th century, when child-mortality gains drove e0 while old-age mortality barely moved [44, 45, 53].\n  - Conversely, AEV would not require period e0 to rise exactly 1 yr/yr.\n\n  See Claim 3 for a formal statement.\n- **Consensus.** No credible demographic, actuarial or biogerontological body treats LEV as an established or expected outcome. It is a speculative hypothesis advocated mainly by de Grey, Kurzweil and associated groups.\n\n**Proposed wording (TSX, line 365-366)**\n\n> (a simplified proxy for “longevity escape velocity”: period life expectancy at birth rising one year per calendar year. De Grey’s original “escape velocity” is a different, stricter test: age-specific death rates falling about 10% a year, so that a living person’s remaining life expectancy grows. LEV is a speculative hypothesis, not a demographic forecast.)\n\n**Proposed wording (`analytics.ts:8-9` comment)**\n\n> // The dashboard uses v(t) >= 1 as a simple *proxy* for “longevity escape\n> // velocity”: period life expectancy at birth rising >= 1 year per calendar\n> // year. This is not de Grey’s actuarial definition (age-specific mortality\n> // falling ~10%/yr so that remaining life expectancy at a given age rises),\n> // and period e0 reaching 1 yr/yr is neither necessary nor sufficient for it.\n\n### 2c. Are gains accelerating or decelerating?\n\n> \"… and the 30-year trend is currently {positive|negative} …\" / \"Extrapolated forward, that trend never crosses the threshold: on the current demographic trajectory, escape velocity is not being approached.\" (`app/src/App.tsx:370-381`)\n\n**Verdict: Confirmed (direction).** It needs context: the latest velocity is COVID-depressed, and the linear ETA can produce spurious dates.\n\n**Evidence from the repository data**\n\n| Series | Velocity at 2023 | 30-yr trend | ETA |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| World | 0.108 | -0.0010 | none |\n| Japan | 0.090 | -0.0026 | none |\n| US | -0.107 | -0.0087 | none |\n| UK | -0.008 | -0.0062 | none |\n| France | 0.057 | -0.0055 | none |\n| China | 0.163 | -0.0075 | none |\n| India | 0.198 | -0.0049 | none |\n| Brazil | -0.031 | -0.0113 | none |\n| Australia | 0.124 | -0.0059 | none |\n| Russia | 0.085 | +0.0378 | ≈2047 |\n| Nigeria | 0.281 | +0.0058 | ≈2147 |\n\n- **The 2023 world velocity is depressed** because the 10-year window spans the COVID dip. Both sides agree that the *maximum* and the *average* move slowly.\n- **Mortality-plateau debate:**\n  - Barbi et al. 2018 (Italy/Denmark/US) [69] reported a hazard plateau after age 105 in 3,836 Italians.\n  - Critiques:\n    - Newman 2018 (Australia/UK): data errors can produce plateaus [70].\n    - Beltrán-Sánchez, Austad & Finch 2018 (US) [71].\n    - Gavrilov & Gavrilova 2019 (US) [72].\n  - Alvarez et al. 2021 (Denmark and others) [73] found results consistent with a plateau in better-validated data from several countries, but with wide uncertainty.\n  - Even if a plateau exists, it is at about 50% annual mortality. That is irrelevant to LEV.\n- **Consensus.** Independent groups in the US, UK, Germany, Denmark and other countries agree:\n  - Current global and best-practice LE gains are about 0.1–0.3 yr/yr, far below 1 yr/yr.\n  - No major forecaster projects acceleration toward 1 yr/yr.\n\n  Whether best-practice gains are slowing (Olshansky) or merely noisy around a linear trend (Vaupel) is genuinely contested.\n\n**Proposed wording (TSX, after the ETA sentence)**\n\n> (Note: the latest value is still depressed by the COVID-19 dip inside the 10-year window; the world gained about 0.25–0.33 years per year in 2000–2019. Positive trends in countries recovering from crises, such as Russia, reflect rebounds, not acceleration toward escape velocity.)\n\n### 2d. \"Breakthroughs in aging biology (senolytics, partial reprogramming, gene therapy) would only register here once they measurably cut death rates at scale.\"\n\n> \"Honest caveat: this instrument measures **period life expectancy** — the mortality of the present, not a forecast. No therapy is approved to slow or reverse human aging. As of 2026, senolytics, partial reprogramming and gene editing have only small, early-phase human studies, mostly on surrogate endpoints and with mixed results, and none has shown a reduction in deaths from aging. Major forecasts (UN World Population Prospects 2024; Global Burden of Disease 2021) project world gains of roughly 0.15 years per year to 2050. Even the best-performing countries have gained only about 0.25 years per year since 1840 (Oeppen & Vaupel 2002; Vaupel et al. 2021). Any future breakthrough would register here only once it measurably cut death rates at scale. The gauge tells us where we are, not what is about to be invented.\n\n### 2e. Methodology text\n\n> \"**Escape velocity:** v(t) ≥ {LEV_THRESHOLD} year of life expectancy per calendar year. The ETA extrapolates the 30-year linear trend of the velocity; it is a trajectory readout, not a prophecy.\" (`app/src/App.tsx:427-429`); \"**Limitation:** period life expectancy summarizes current death rates. A true immortality probability would need cohort projections and biological-aging biomarkers\" (`:432-434`)\n\n**Verdict: Confirmed (limitation) / Corrected (escape-velocity definition is a proxy).**\n\n**Evidence:** see 2b and Claim 3. The limitation statement agrees with standard demography: period LE is a synthetic summary of one year's death rates [31, 53].\n\n\"Biological-aging biomarkers\" should be qualified as not yet validated [103, 104].\n\n**Proposed wording**\n\n> - **Escape velocity (proxy):** v(t) ≥ {LEV_THRESHOLD} year of period life expectancy at birth per calendar year. This is a simplification of de Grey’s “actuarial escape velocity”, which requires age-specific death rates to fall about 10% per year. The ETA linearly extrapolates the 30-year trend of the velocity. Rebounds after wars, famines or pandemics can produce spurious ETAs; it is a trajectory readout, not a prophecy. The latest data year is 2023.\n> - **Limitation:** period life expectancy summarizes current death rates. A true immortality probability would need cohort projections and age-specific mortality trends. Biological-aging biomarkers (epigenetic clocks) are not yet validated as surrogate endpoints. This dashboard deliberately sticks to what is actually measured today.\n\n---\n\n## Claim 3: the core metric, LEV as period LE gain ≥ 1 yr/yr\n\n> `export const LEV_THRESHOLD = 1;` (`app/src/analytics.ts:16`), applied to v(t) = d e0(t)/dt, where e0 is period life expectancy at birth (`app/src/analytics.ts:3-9`, `App.tsx:427-429`)\n\n**Verdict: Corrected (it is a proxy, not the definition). The current-rate finding is Confirmed: about 0.1 yr/yr now and about 0.25–0.33 pre-COVID, far below 1.**\n\n**Formal analysis**\n\nLet μ(x, t) be the death rate at age x in year t. Let e_x(t) be period remaining life expectancy at age x.\n\n- **De Grey's actuarial escape velocity** [31] concerns a living person aged x in year t. Their remaining life expectancy should not shrink as they age:\n\n  e_{x+1}(t+1) ≥ e_x(t).\n\n  For adult mortality that roughly follows a Gompertz curve with slope b, this requires\n\n  -∂ ln μ / ∂t ≥ b,\n\n  i.e. age-specific death rates falling about 8–10% per year at the ages where most deaths occur. De Grey says \"about 10% per year\".\n- **Historical rates.** Old-age mortality has fallen by about 1–2% per year in the best-performing countries since the 1950s. This is shown by Kannisto et al. 1994 (Denmark/US, 27 countries) [53] and Vaupel 2010 [39]. That is roughly a tenth of the required rate.\n- **Period e0 rising 1 yr/yr is not equivalent.**\n  1. e0 is heavily weighted by infant and child deaths. Eliminating child mortality can raise e0 very fast (several yr/yr in rebounds) without changing e_x for adults.\n  2. Conversely, rejuvenation that cut adult μ by 10%/yr would raise e0 by an amount depending on the age structure of deaths. That need not be exactly 1 yr/yr at the moment AEV is reached.\n  3. Period measures lag cohort reality when mortality is falling. Cohort life expectancy exceeds period life expectancy in that case [34].\n\n  So the threshold d e0/dt ≥ 1 is neither necessary nor sufficient for AEV. It is, however, a reasonable *order-of-magnitude* sanity check: if e0 rises much more slowly than 1 yr/yr, AEV is clearly not being reached.\n- **Better formalisations the dashboard could add later** (suggestions only; nothing was implemented here):\n  - Annual % decline in age-specific death rates at ages 60–90, compared with about 10%/yr.\n  - The change in e65 or e80 per calendar year, compared with the roughly 1-year-per-year decrease in e_x from ageing one year.\n\n  Both are computable from the Human Mortality Database, not from the OWID e0 series currently used.\n\n**Current world rate**\n\n- Repository data: 2023 velocity 0.108 yr/yr (COVID-affected window); 2000–2019 ≈ 0.33 yr/yr; 2010–2019 ≈ 0.25 yr/yr.\n- UN WPP 2024 [42]: world LE 72.6 (2019), 70.9 (2021), 73.3 (2024). That is a full rebound past the pre-COVID level by 2024. The repository snapshot (73.17 in 2023) does not yet include 2024.\n- Forecasts:\n  - GBD 2021 [40]: ≈0.16 yr/yr to 2050.\n  - UN WPP 2024 [42]: ≈0.14 yr/yr to 2054.\n- **Consensus.** UN DESA, IHME/GBD, MPIDR, and the Olshansky and Vaupel groups all put current or projected gains between about 0.1 and 0.3 yr/yr. No independent source projects 1 yr/yr.\n\n**Proposed wording:** see 2b (`analytics.ts` comment and verdict parenthesis) and 2e (methodology).\n\n---\n\n## Items that could not be verified (stated explicitly)\n\n1. **The Nature Biotechnology article cited by the CRISPR document** (doi:10.1038/s41587-023-02415-8). The 30-year trend is currently …\n349\t\n350\t### 2b. Longevity escape velocity: consensus or hypothesis?\n351\t\n352\t> \"(the point where each calendar year lived adds a full year of life expectancy, so remaining life expectancy stops shrinking)\" (`app/src/App.tsx:365-366`); \"Longevity escape velocity (LEV) is the point where v(t) >= 1: every calendar year lived adds at least one more year of remaining life expectancy.\" (`app/src/analytics.ts:8-9`)\n353\t\n354\t**Verdict: Speculative** (the concept), and **Corrected** (the definition used).\n355\t\n356\t**Evidence**\n357\t\n358\t- **Origin.**\n359\t  - The concept comes from Aubrey de Grey (UK/US; de Grey 2004, PLoS Biology) [31], building on the SENS programme [32].\n360\t  - Ray Kurzweil popularised it and predicts LEV around 2029–2035 [80].\n361\t  - Neither is a demographic forecast based on mortality data.\n362\t- **No peer-reviewed demographic forecast predicts LEV this century.**\n363\t  - Major forecasting groups project world gains of about 0.14–0.16 yr/yr to 2050:\n364\t    - UN Population Division [42]\n365\t    - IHME / GBD, US with global collaborators [40]\n366\t  - High-longevity forecasts reach about 0.25 yr/yr. Examples are Oeppen & Vaupel's record-LE trend (UK/Germany/Denmark) [33] and Vaupel et al. 2021 [34].\n367\t  - Olshansky et al. 2024 (US) [35] argue gains are decelerating and that radical life extension is \"implausible\" this century unless aging itself is slowed. That is a scenario no one can yet forecast.\n368\t- **Critique by gerontologists.** In 2005, 28 senior biogerontologists from several countries published a detailed rebuttal of the SENS agenda [37]. They did not rule out future progress, but rejected claims of imminent indefinite life extension.\n369\t- **What de Grey actually defined.** He defined the threshold in terms of **age-specific mortality**, not period life expectancy at birth [31]. His words:\n370\t\n371\t  > \"mortality rates fall so fast that people's remaining (not merely total) life expectancy increases with time … the ratio of the mortality rates at consecutive ages (in the same year) in the age range where most people die, which is only about 10% per year. I term this rate of reduction of age-specific mortality risk 'actuarial escape velocity' (AEV).\"\n372\t\n373\t  He also calls period life expectancy \"a purely artificial construction\".\n374\t- **Why \"remaining life expectancy stops shrinking\" does not follow from period e0 rising 1 yr/yr.**\n375\t  - Period e0 is dominated by deaths at young ages.\n376\t  - An individual's remaining life expectancy is e at their *current* age x, evaluated over their own future.\n377\t  - One year later, the relevant quantity is e at age x+1 in year t+1. It can keep falling even while e0 rises fast, as happened in the mid-20th century, when child-mortality gains drove e0 while old-age mortality barely moved [44, 45, 53].\n378\t  - Conversely, AEV would not require period e0 to rise exactly 1 yr/yr.\n379\t\n380\t  See Claim 3 for a formal statement.\n381\t- **Consensus.** No credible demographic, actuarial or biogerontological body treats LEV as an established or expected outcome. It is a speculative hypothesis advocated mainly by de Grey, Kurzweil and associated groups.\n382\t\n383\t**Proposed wording (TSX, line 365-366)**\n384\t\n385\t> (a simplified proxy for “longevity escape velocity”: period life expectancy at birth rising one year per calendar year. De Grey’s original “escape velocity” is a different, stricter test: age-specific death rates falling about 10% a year, so that a living person’s remaining life expectancy grows. LEV is a speculative hypothesis, not a demographic forecast.)\n386\t\n387\t**Proposed wording (`analytics.ts:8-9` comment)**\n388\t\n389\t> // The dashboard uses v(t) >= 1 as a simple *proxy* for “longevity escape\n390\t> // velocity”: period life expectancy at birth rising >= 1 year per calendar\n391\t> // year. This is not de Grey’s actuarial definition (age-specific mortality\n392\t> // falling ~10%/yr so that remaining life expectancy at a given age rises),\n393\t> // and period e0 reaching 1 yr/yr is neither necessary nor sufficient for it.\n394\t\n395\t### 2c. That is irrelevant to LEV.\n470\t- **Consensus.** Independent groups in the US, UK, Germany, Denmark and other countries agree:\n471\t  - Current global and best-practice LE gains are about 0.1–0.3 yr/yr, far below 1 yr/yr.\n472\t  - No major forecaster projects acceleration toward 1 yr/yr.\n473\t\n474\t  Whether best-practice gains are slowing (Olshansky) or merely noisy around a linear trend (Vaupel) is genuinely contested.\n475\t\n476\t**Proposed wording (TSX, after the ETA sentence)**\n477\t\n478\t> (Note: the latest value is still depressed by the COVID-19 dip inside the 10-year window; the world gained about 0.25–0.33 years per year in 2000–2019. As of October 2026:\n485\t\n486\t- No therapy is approved for aging.\n487\t- No aging-targeted intervention has shown an all-cause mortality reduction in a randomised trial.\n488\t\n489\t**Evidence (state of human evidence, October 2026)**\n490\t\n491\t- **Senolytics.**\n492\t  - Unity Biotechnology's UBX0101 failed its Phase 2 trial in knee osteoarthritis (2020) [75].\n493\t  - UBX1325 (ASPIRE, diabetic macular oedema) missed its primary non-inferiority endpoint. In June 2025 Unity's board approved dissolution of the company [76]. The outcome of the stockholder vote was not verified.\n494\t  - Mayo Clinic and other US groups have run small dasatinib plus quercetin studies:\n495\t    - diabetic kidney disease, n=9, open-label [77]\n496\t    - idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, n=14, open-label [78]\n497\t    - mild Alzheimer's, n=5, Phase 1 [79]\n498\t  - The largest RCT, in postmenopausal women (n=60), missed its primary bone endpoint (P=0.611). It showed only an exploratory benefit in the highest-senescence tertile [74].\n499\t  - **Status:** small, mostly single-centre US studies with mixed results; **no replicated efficacy**.\n500\t- **Partial reprogramming.**\n501\t  - Animal evidence:\n502\t    - Ocampo et al. 2016 (US/Spain): cyclic OSKM in progeroid mice [81].\n503\t    - Lu et al. 2020 (US/international): OSK restores vision in mouse glaucoma and aging models [82].\n504\t  - First in human: Life Biosciences ER-100 (intravitreal, inducible OSK; NCT07290244). The first patient was dosed on 9 Jun 2026 [83].\n505\t  - Company-reported interim data from 8 Oct 2026 [84]:\n506\t    - 3 glaucoma participants\n507\t    - well tolerated to day 56, with no dose-limiting toxicities or serious adverse events\n508\t    - visual-field improvement in 2 of 3\n509\t\n510\t    These data are not peer-reviewed. Status: **Unconfirmed-single-study** (3 patients, one sponsor).\n511\t  - The human-trial status of Altos Labs and Retro Biosciences was **not verified** in this review.\n512\t- **Gene therapy.**\n513\t  - Approved gene therapies (Casgevy and others) treat monogenic diseases, not aging (Claim 1).\n514\t  - No gene therapy for aging has peer-reviewed human efficacy data. Unregulated \"longevity gene therapy\" self-experiments are anecdotes, not evidence.\n515\t- **Rapamycin / mTOR inhibitors.**\n516\t  - In older adults, low-dose mTOR inhibition improved vaccine response [85].\n517\t  - Mannick et al. 2021 [86]: a Phase 2b trial positive; the Phase 3 (RTB101) missed its primary endpoint.\n518\t  - The PEARL trial (48 weeks, low-dose intermittent; Moel et al. 2025 [87]) was null on its primary visceral-fat endpoint. It showed some secondary benefits in women.\n519\t- **Metformin.**\n520\t  - The TAME trial [88] is designed for 3,000 participants aged 65–79 over about 6 years. As of 2024 it was still not fully funded [89]. No primary source confirming enrollment as of 2026 was found.\n521\t  - Observational evidence conflicts:\n522\t    - Bannister et al. 2014 (UK): a survival advantage over non-diabetic controls [90].\n523\t    - Keys et al. 2022 (Denmark, including twin analyses): no such advantage [91].\n524\t  - RCTs show metformin blunts exercise adaptations in older adults (Konopka 2019; Walton 2019, US) [92, 93].\n525\t- **GLP-1 receptor agonists.**\n526\t  - SELECT (semaglutide in obesity without diabetes, 41 countries) [94]: all-cause death HR 0.81 (0.71–0.93). This was not formally significance-tested, because the hierarchical CV-death endpoint failed (HR 0.85).\n527\t  - FLOW (semaglutide in diabetic kidney disease) [95] and a meta-analysis of 8 cardiovascular outcome trials [96] support lower mortality **in disease populations**.\n528\t  - None of these is an aging indication.\n529\t- **Biomarkers (\"biological age clocks\").**\n530\t  - Main clocks: Horvath (US) [97], Hannum (US) [98], PhenoAge [99], GrimAge [100], DunedinPACE (US/NZ/UK) [101].\n531\t  - They predict mortality in many cohorts.\n532\t  - Reliability concerns: Higgins-Chen et al. 2022 [102].\n533\t  - Expert consortium statements (Moqri et al. 2023, 2024; international) say no aging biomarker is yet validated as a surrogate endpoint for regulatory use [103, 104].\n534\t  - CALERIE, the caloric-restriction RCT [105], slowed DunedinPACE modestly but not other clocks.\n535\t- **Framework.** The hallmarks-of-aging framework (López-Otín et al. 2023, Spain/France/US) [106] guides research. It is not evidence that any intervention works in humans.\n536\t- **Consensus.** Across the US, UK, Europe and other regions:\n537\t  - No regulator has approved any therapy for aging.\n538\t  - No aging-targeted drug has replicated, randomised evidence of extending human lifespan or cutting all-cause mortality in the general older population.\n539\t\n540\t**Proposed replacement text for the caveat (TSX, lines 385-389)**\n541\t\n542\t> Honest caveat: this instrument measures **period life expectancy** — the mortality of the present, not a forecast. “Longevity escape velocity” is a speculative hypothesis, not a scientific consensus. No therapy is approved to slow or reverse human aging. As of 2026, senolytics, partial reprogramming and gene editing have only small, early-phase human studies, mostly on surrogate endpoints and with mixed results, and none has shown a reduction in deaths from aging. Major forecasts (UN World Population Prospects 2024; Global Burden of Disease 2021) project world gains of roughly 0.15 years per year to 2050. Even the best-performing countries have gained only about 0.25 years per year since 1840 (Oeppen & Vaupel 2002; Vaupel et al. 2021). Any future breakthrough would register here only once it measurably cut death rates at scale. The gauge tells us where we are, not what is about to be invented.\n543\t\n544\t### 2e. Methodology text\n545\t\n546\t> \"**Escape velocity:** v(t) ≥ {LEV_THRESHOLD} year of life expectancy per calendar year. The ETA extrapolates the 30-year linear trend of the velocity; it is a trajectory readout, not a prophecy.\" (`app/src/App.tsx:427-429`); \"**Limitation:** period life expectancy summarizes current death rates. A true immortality probability would need cohort projections and biological-aging biomarkers\" (`:432-434`)\n547\t\n548\t**Verdict: Confirmed (limitation) / Corrected (escape-velocity definition is a proxy).**\n549\t\n550\t**Evidence:** see 2b and Claim 3. The limitation statement agrees with standard demography: period LE is a synthetic summary of one year's death rates [31, 53].\n551\t\n552\t\"Biological-aging biomarkers\" should be qualified as not yet validated [103, 104].\n553\t\n554\t**Proposed wording**\n555\t\n556\t> - **Escape velocity (proxy):** v(t) ≥ {LEV_THRESHOLD} year of period life expectancy at birth per calendar year. This is a simplification of de Grey’s “actuarial escape velocity”, which requires age-specific death rates to fall about 10% per year. The ETA linearly extrapolates the 30-year trend of the velocity. Rebounds after wars, famines or pandemics can produce spurious ETAs; it is a trajectory readout, not a prophecy. The latest data year is 2023.\n557\t> - **Limitation:** period life expectancy summarizes current death rates. A true immortality probability would need cohort projections and age-specific mortality trends. Biological-aging biomarkers (epigenetic clocks) are not yet validated as surrogate endpoints. This dashboard deliberately sticks to what is actually measured today.\n558\t\n559\t---\n560\t\n561\t## Claim 3: the core metric, LEV as period LE gain ≥ 1 yr/yr\n562\t\n563\t> `export const LEV_THRESHOLD = 1;` (`app/src/analytics.ts:16`), applied to v(t) = d e0(t)/dt, where e0 is period life expectancy at birth (`app/src/analytics.ts:3-9`, `App.tsx:427-429`)\n564\t\n565\t**Verdict: Corrected (it is a proxy, not the definition). The current-rate finding is Confirmed: about 0.1 yr/yr now and about 0.25–0.33 pre-COVID, far below 1.**\n566\t\n567\t**Formal analysis**\n568\t\n569\tLet μ(x, t) be the death rate at age x in year t. Let e_x(t) be period remaining life expectancy at age x.\n570\t\n571\t- **De Grey's actuarial escape velocity** [31] concerns a living person aged x in year t. Their remaining life expectancy should not shrink as they age:\n572\t\n573\t  e_{x+1}(t+1) ≥ e_x(t).\n574\t\n575\t  For adult mortality that roughly follows a Gompertz curve with slope b, this requires\n576\t\n577\t  -∂ ln μ / ∂t ≥ b,\n578\t\n579\t  i.e. age-specific death rates falling about 8–10% per year at the ages where most deaths occur. De Grey says \"about 10% per year\".\n580\t- **Historical rates.** Old-age mortality has fallen by about 1–2% per year in the best-performing countries since the 1950s. This is shown by Kannisto et al. 1994 (Denmark/US, 27 countries) [53] and Vaupel 2010 [39]. That is roughly a tenth of the required rate.\n581\t- **Period e0 rising 1 yr/yr is not equivalent.**\n582\t  1. e0 is heavily weighted by infant and child deaths. Eliminating child mortality can raise e0 very fast (several yr/yr in rebounds) without changing e_x for adults.\n583\t  2. Conversely, rejuvenation that cut adult μ by 10%/yr would raise e0 by an amount depending on the age structure of deaths. That need not be exactly 1 yr/yr at the moment AEV is reached.\n584\t  3. Period measures lag cohort reality when mortality is falling. Cohort life expectancy exceeds period life expectancy in that case [34].\n585\t\n586\t  So the threshold d e0/dt ≥ 1 is neither necessary nor sufficient for AEV. It is, however, a reasonable *order-of-magnitude* sanity check: if e0 rises much more slowly than 1 yr/yr, AEV is clearly not being reached.\n587\t- **Better formalisations the dashboard could add later** (suggestions only; nothing was implemented here):\n588\t  - Annual % decline in age-specific death rates at ages 60–90, compared with about 10%/yr.\n589\t  - The change in e65 or e80 per calendar year, compared with the roughly 1-year-per-year decrease in e_x from ageing one year.\n590\t\n591\t  Both are computable from the Human Mortality Database, not from the OWID e0 series currently used.\n592\t\n593\t**Current world rate**\n594\t\n595\t- Repository data: 2023 velocity 0.108 yr/yr (COVID-affected window); 2000–2019 ≈ 0.33 yr/yr; 2010–2019 ≈ 0.25 yr/yr.\n596\t- UN WPP 2024 [42]: world LE 72.6 (2019), 70.9 (2021), 73.3 (2024). That is a full rebound past the pre-COVID level by 2024. The repository snapshot (73.17 in 2023) does not yet include 2024.\n597\t- Forecasts:\n598\t  - GBD 2021 [40]: ≈0.16 yr/yr to 2050.\n599\t  - UN WPP 2024 [42]: ≈0.14 yr/yr to 2054.\n600\t- **Consensus.** UN DESA, IHME/GBD, MPIDR, and the Olshansky and Vaupel groups all put current or projected gains between about 0.1 and 0.3 yr/yr. No independent source projects 1 yr/yr.\n601\t\n602\t**Proposed wording:** see 2b (`analytics.ts` comment and verdict parenthesis) and 2e (methodology).\n603\t\n604\t---\n605\t\n606\t## Items that could not be verified (stated explicitly)\n607\t"
